lessons.title: Share ownership, check mutation
lessons.task: Try to increment the shared counter. Return false if it is currently borrowed, without panicking.
lessons.hint: Match try_borrow_mut and mutate through the guard only on success.
body: Rc clones share an allocation by updating a non-atomic reference count; cloning Rc<T> does not clone T. Rc is for one thread. Arc provides atomic reference counting when shared ownership must cross threads.

RefCell moves borrowing checks to runtime. Conflicting borrow_mut calls panic; try_borrow_mut reports failure instead. This flexibility has bookkeeping cost and does not provide thread synchronization.
Keep guards short-lived. The exercise makes a live immutable borrow block a mutation, then succeeds when that guard is dropped. Reference cycles can leak; Weak is useful for non-owning back edges.

lessons.title: Borrow across a thread boundary
lessons.task: Split the input in half; sum each half in a scoped worker and join both results.
lessons.hint: Use thread::scope and join the two handles inside its closure.
body: Scoped threads must finish before their scope returns, allowing them to borrow stack-owned data safely. This can avoid cloning a large input just to satisfy a detached thread’s static lifetime requirement.

Send means ownership may be transferred between threads; Sync means shared references may cross threads. These auto traits encode safety requirements, not a promise of contention-free or fast execution.
Spawning OS threads has overhead. This tiny example teaches ownership, not a speedup: for small inputs a serial sum will usually be the better choice. Reuse a worker pool for repeated parallel work.

lessons.title: A counter is not a publication protocol
lessons.task: Spawn four scoped workers; each increments one shared atomic counter n times. Return the total after joining.
lessons.hint: Use AtomicUsize::fetch_add with Relaxed; scope joins before the final load.
body: Atomic read-modify-write operations prevent lost updates to one atomic value. Relaxed ordering supplies atomicity without ordering unrelated memory accesses. It can be appropriate for an independent statistic.

A flag that publishes other data needs a properly designed synchronization protocol, often a Release store paired with an Acquire load that observes it. Simply changing every load to Relaxed can break that protocol.
Even relaxed atomics can contend on a cache line. Per-worker counters followed by reduction may scale better. Here thread joins establish completion before we inspect the final counter.
